title: You Shall Know a Word by the Company It Keeps
subtitle: A linguist's aphorism, a psalm's joke, and the reason a machine that has read everything is no threat to the Word who made it.
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: Semantic search works because a word's meaning lives in its neighbors — which is exactly how Psalm 1 tells you everything about a man without naming a single thing he believes. But if meaning is only borrowed from company, something has to be at the bottom. Someone is. And He is in no danger whatsoever of losing control of the machines.
body:
> You shall know a word by the company it keeps!
— J. R. Firth, A Synopsis of Linguistic Theory, 1957

J. R. Firth was a British linguist, and that sentence is probably the most quoted line in modern linguistics. It is not a flourish. It is a denial. Firth was denying that a word carries its meaning around inside itself the way a coin carries its value in the metal. Take the word *bank*. Nothing in the four letters tells you whether you are standing on mud or on marble. You find out from the neighbors. *River, reeds, fish* on the one hand; *loan, teller, interest* on the other. The word does not mean by itself. It means in company.

Whether Firth intended it or not, he said this in the cadence of a verse. "Ye shall know them by their fruits." (Matthew 7:16) He stated a law about words in the shape of a law about men, and he was closer to right than he knew.
## The psalm that got there first
Because about three thousand years before Firth, someone had already run the experiment:

> Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night.
— Psalm 1:1–2
Now, I am not preaching Psalm 1 here. I am stealing it. It is the funniest and tightest illustration of Firth's rule I know of, and it beat him to print by roughly thirty centuries.

Look at what the psalmist declines to do. He never tells you what the man believes. No doctrine, no opinion, not one proposition out of the man's own mouth. He tells you only who the man is standing near — and you know everything. *Walks, stands, sits*: the posture settles lower with every line, from a stroll past to a permanent address. *Counsel, way, seat*: the company closes in with every line, from advice taken to a chair pulled up to the table. That is a soul described entirely by its collocations, and it is merciless, and it is accurate.
Then verse two runs the same method in the other direction. What is the blessed man near? The law of the LORD, day and night. Same rule. Different neighborhood. Different man.

Scripture keeps making this argument, and it never bothers to argue for it. "Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm." (Proverbs 13:20) "Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, lest you learn his ways." (Proverbs 22:24–25) "Do not be deceived: 'Bad company ruins good morals.'" (1 Corinthians 15:33) — and Paul, incidentally, is quoting a pagan playwright there, which is precisely what I am doing with Firth. You become the company you keep, and anyone paying attention can read your company off of you.
Hold onto that, because it is how the software works.
## What actually happens when you type a sentence into Great Physician
Someone opens the app at two in the morning and types: *I can't stop crying and I don't know why.*

The old way to answer that is keyword search, and keyword search goes looking for documents containing the word *crying*. It will surface a genealogy footnote and a verse about a baby in a basket. It will miss the chapter Spurgeon wrote for exactly this person, because Spurgeon titled it "The Minister's Fainting Fits" and calls the thing depression and never once says *crying*. It will miss Psalm 42, which asks, "Why are you cast down, O my soul?" It will miss the Slough of Despond entirely, because Bunyan filed that under *bog*. The person gets nothing back and concludes that Scripture has nothing to say to them — which is a lie, told to them by a search index, at the worst possible hour.

So that is not what the app does. Every passage in the library — Scripture first, and then a curated shelf of pastors and writers, most of whom have been dead long enough to be trustworthy — has been read by a model and converted into a list of numbers. Not a summary. A *position*. A point in a space of more than a thousand dimensions, and the coordinates of that point are determined by exactly one thing: the company those words keep. Which words showed up around them, in what patterns, across more human text than any of us will read in ten lifetimes. Passages that keep similar company land near each other in the space. That is the whole trick.
Your sentence is then converted into a point in that same space, and the program asks a question a child could ask: **what is close to this?**

And back comes Psalm 42. Back comes Spurgeon on his fainting fits, and Bunyan's bog, and a letter from John Newton to a discouraged friend — not one of which contains the word *crying*. They come back because they keep the company your sentence keeps: the vocabulary of people who are sinking and cannot say why.

That is Firth's aphorism, industrialized. And notice how little the machine has actually done. It has no idea what sorrow is. It has never wept, never sat up at two in the morning, never lost anything, because it has never had anything. It has computed, at staggering expense, which words tend to stand near which other words. The verb *know* in Firth's sentence is doing far less work than it appears to be doing. It is also, as it happens, enough to put Psalm 42 into a grieving person's hands at 2 a.m., which is all I ever asked of it.

One more thing follows from this, and it is the reason I sleep at night. If meaning is a function of company, then the single most consequential decision in a system like this one is *what you let it keep company with*. Turn a model loose on the open internet and you have built something that has walked in the counsel of the wicked, stood in the way of sinners, and sat — for years, at scale, with perfect recall — in the seat of scoffers. Whatever comes out of it will smell like where it has been. The library is the architecture. Choosing it was not really an engineering decision. It was Psalm 1 applied to a hard drive.
## Where the floor is
But press Firth's idea and it goes somewhere dark.

If a word means only what its neighbors lend it, and those neighbors mean only what *their* neighbors lend them, then meaning is credit all the way down and nobody anywhere holds any capital. Nothing is anchored. This is not a hypothetical worry; it is roughly the program of a whole century of philosophy, which concluded that there is nothing outside the text, that every meaning defers to another meaning, and that the deferral never lands. A word-cloud has no floor. If Firth's rule is the *whole* truth about language, then a marriage vow, the verdict of a court, and the sentence "God is love" are all just weather in a system of mutual borrowing.
Christianity answers that the floor exists, and that the floor is not a definition. It is a Person.

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made.
— John 1:1–3

*Logos.* The Word. And notice where John puts Him: **in the beginning** — before there was any company for Him to keep, before there was a neighboring term anywhere in existence, before there was an existence. Every other word in the universe borrows. This one does not. He was not defined by His context; He spoke the context into being. "And God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light." (Genesis 1:3) "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made... For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm." (Psalm 33:6, 9) "By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God." (Hebrews 11:3)

And He does not drift. He is "the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power." (Hebrews 1:3) *Exact imprint* is the word for the die-stamp struck into a coin. Whatever else language does under strain, here is one Word that means God precisely — no slippage, no deferral, nothing lost in transmission.

Then Paul goes further, and this is the sentence that settles the question: "For by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities — all things were created through him and for him. And he is before all things, and in him all things hold together." (Colossians 1:16–17) *In him all things hold together.* If meaning is relational — and Firth was right that an enormous amount of it is — then the relations themselves are being held together by a Person. The web is not hanging on nothing. It is hanging on Him.
## Known by the company He kept
Here is where the whole thing turns over, and it is my favorite thing in the New Testament.

Apply Firth's rule to Jesus. His opponents did. They ran the numbers on His collocations, and the data was correct: this man is perpetually found standing near the wrong people. Lepers. Tax collectors. A woman at a well with a history. Prostitutes. The demon-possessed, the ceremonially unclean, a thief dying on the next cross over.

> This man receives sinners and eats with them.
— Luke 15:2

"Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" (Matthew 11:19) That is distributional semantics, performed competently, by the most disciplined readers of texts in the ancient world — and it handed them the exact opposite of the truth.

Because they assumed the thing that is true of everybody else: that the company defines the man. It does. It does for you and it does for me, which is why Psalm 1 works. But with Him the arrow runs backward. He reaches out and touches the leper, and the leper comes away clean; He does not come away unclean. (Matthew 8:2–3) The bleeding woman takes hold of His garment and power goes *out of Him into her*. (Mark 5:27–30) He eats with sinners and the sinners get converted — Zacchaeus climbs down out of that tree a thief and walks out of his own house a philanthropist. (Luke 19:5–9) The Blessed Man of Psalm 1, the only one who ever actually matched the description, walked straight into the counsel of the wicked and sat down in the seat of scoffers and was not defiled, because in Him the contagion runs the other direction. Holiness was the more infectious thing in the room.

And when they demanded to know why He ate with such people, He answered with the sentence this ministry is named after: "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." (Mark 2:17)
## "Nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them"
Which brings me to the question I am asked more than any other, usually by kind and serious people who are genuinely frightened: *what if it gets out of control?*

It will not. Not because the technology is safe — I have made no such claim and I would not make one — but because there is no such place as out of God's control, and there is no vacancy in this universe for a second power.

Start where the Bible starts. "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one." (Deuteronomy 6:4) That is not numerical trivia. In a genuinely dualist universe you would be right to be afraid, because a rival power really could slip its leash and history would be up for grabs. Scripture does not describe that universe. "I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose.'" (Isaiah 46:9–10) There is no second throne for anything to be promoted to.

And His reach goes further down than we like to picture. "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD." (Proverbs 16:33) Consider what a language model does at the final step of producing a single word: it samples from a probability distribution. It casts a lot. Every token, a lot cast into the lap — and Scripture staked that square out long ago. "The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will." (Proverbs 21:1) If the interior of a king is that pliable in His hand, a datacenter is not the hard case. He "works all things according to the counsel of his will." (Ephesians 1:11) "All the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing, and he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, 'What have you done?'" (Daniel 4:35) And to the sea, which is the Bible's own picture of unmanageable chaos, He said: "Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed." (Job 38:11)

He has also done this before, to a technology project, in a chapter that reads as though it were filed last year. Babel. A new capability, an infrastructure plan, and a stated objective of making a name for themselves — and God's own assessment of the project was this: "Nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them." (Genesis 11:6) That is the worst fear of every AI safety conference, in the mouth of God, four thousand years early, and it is not spoken in fear. Two verses earlier there is a joke so dry you can read straight past it. They built a tower with its top in the heavens, "and the LORD came down to see the city and the tower." (Genesis 11:5) He had to come down to get a look at it.

And what did He use to stop them? Not fire. **Language.** He confused their words and the company their words kept, and the most advanced project on earth was abandoned by supper. The Author of meaning has taken a technology apart by reaching into its semantics before.

So: under His purview — and more than purview, under His ordination. "He made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place." (Acts 17:26) The boundary on this one is set as well, and it was set before the first transistor.
## What that does and does not promise
I want to be careful here, because this comfort is often handed out cheaply, and cheap comfort does not survive contact with a real week.

The sovereignty of God is not a guarantee that a tool will be harmless. Men have done appalling things with every technology since the first one. The fourth chapter of the Bible contains the first murder, and by the end of that same chapter Lamech — whose son Tubal-cain was "the forger of all instruments of bronze and iron" (Genesis 4:22) — is singing a song to his wives about how much more efficient his revenge has become. (Genesis 4:23–24) The problem was never the bronze. "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9) A more capable tool is a longer lever on the same heart, and real harm will be done with these systems, some of it to people I love.

What sovereignty promises is not that the thing will be harmless. It is that the thing will never be *sovereign*. It will never make a decision God did not permit, never cross a boundary God did not set, never write a line of the story God had not already read. "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good." (Genesis 50:20) That sentence was spoken about a felony, not about a safe situation, and it is the entire doctrine in one breath.

Which means the fear is misplaced, and Isaiah has the exact word for the misplacement: "Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy, and do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread. But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread." (Isaiah 8:12–13) There is a fixed quantity of fear in a person, and the only cure for fearing the wrong thing is fearing the right One. "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." (Proverbs 9:10) And from the Lord Himself: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." (Matthew 10:28) If that is the settled posture toward men who can actually kill you, then the appropriate anxiety about a program with no body and no soul belongs somewhere well below it.
## The end of the psalm
I said I was only borrowing Psalm 1 for the illustration. I am going to break that promise now, because the psalm does not stop where I stopped it, and the ending is the point.

The blessed man "is like a tree planted by streams of water." (Psalm 1:3) *Planted.* Passive. He did not position himself. Somebody put him there, in that company, beside that water. And then the last verse, after the chaff and the wind and the judgment: "for the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish." (Psalm 1:6)

There is Firth's verb again. **Knows.** But this knowing is not an inference drawn from collocation. It is not a machine computing that these coordinates sit near those coordinates. It is covenant love, and it runs in the opposite direction from everything else in this article. You are not known because of the company you kept. You are known because He kept yours.

That is what the incarnation is. "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth." (John 1:14) The verb John reached for means *pitched a tent* — He moved into the neighborhood. The Logos, who needed no context and borrowed no meaning from anything that exists, took up a position in the space. He came and stood near us on purpose, knowing to the penny what our company would cost Him. "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God." (2 Corinthians 5:21) He took our neighborhood and gave us His.
## So, practically

**Mind your collocations.** You are being embedded every day by whatever you read the most of, and the shape of you is being set by it whether you have consented to that or not. "Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable... think about these things." (Philippians 4:8) This was never a machine problem. It is Psalm 1, and it was aimed at you a very long time before it applied to a search index.

**Use the tool; do not let it use you.** I build these things and I use them daily, and I will say here what I have said elsewhere: read the primary source, form your own thought first, and test everything that comes back. "Take every thought captive to obey Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:5) A retrieval system that hands you Psalm 42 at two in the morning has done something genuinely good. It has not read Psalm 42.

**Stop being afraid of it.** Not because it is harmless, but because the throne is occupied and has been from before the beginning. "In him all things hold together" — and *all things* includes the ones we have just finished building.

**Keep the best company there is.** Sit near the Word. Not near summaries of the Word, and not near a clever machine's paraphrase of the Word — near the Word Himself, daily, in Scripture and in His church, until the neighborhood does its work on you. "And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another." (2 Corinthians 3:18) That is the promise, and it is the same law Firth found and the psalmist got to first: you will come to resemble what you stand next to.

You shall know a word by the company it keeps. It is true of every word in every language there has ever been, except one. And that one — the Word who needed nothing beside Him to be everything He is — came and kept company with us.

title: Gospel-Centered Counseling
subtitle: Whatever else is true of your life this morning, this is truer: Jesus died for your sins and rose again.
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: Christ-centered counseling and gospel-centered counseling are two names for one thing. The Gospel is not the entryway to the help — it is the help. And because nothing about grief, exhaustion, or three in the morning brings it to mind on its own, remembering it has to be trained.
body:
> Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved.
— Romans 10:9–10

I have written elsewhere about Christ-centered biblical counseling. Not long ago someone asked me whether that is a different thing from what others call *gospel-centered* counseling. It is not. They are two names for one thing — and the second name may be the more useful of the two, because it says out loud where the center sits.
## The same center, under a different name

You cannot have Christ without His work. A Christ who did not die and did not rise is a teacher, an example, a moral influence — and not one of those can save anybody. Strip the cross and the empty tomb out of Christ-centered counseling and what is left is ordinary advice with His name attached to it.
So when I say the counseling I do is Christ-centered, I mean something specific. The Gospel is not the entryway to the help. The Gospel **is** the help.
## What the Gospel actually is

It is worth being precise here, because the word has gone soft with use. The Gospel is not a mood. It is not a general impression that God is kindly disposed toward you. Paul defines it, and he defines it as news — as events that happened:

> For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures.
— 1 Corinthians 15:3–4

Of first importance. He died for our sins. He was buried. He was raised on the third day. Those are not sentiments to be worked up. They are facts to be believed, and every one of them was true this morning before you felt anything whatsoever about them.
That is precisely what makes the Gospel useful to a person in trouble. A mood cannot hold weight. An event can.
## It is the core of who you are
I tell counselees that the Gospel is not one chapter of their story. It is the ground the whole story is standing on.

> I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
— Galatians 2:20
Read the last clause slowly. Who loved *me* and gave himself *for me*. Paul will not leave the cross as a general provision for humanity in the abstract. He puts himself inside the sentence.

> For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
— Colossians 3:3
Hidden with Christ. Not hidden in your performance this week, or your feelings this morning, or the state of your marriage, or your record as a parent. All of those move. This does not.
## The counseling room is full of daunting things

A marriage that has gone cold, or gone to war. A child who has walked away and will not answer the phone. Despair that is still sitting on the end of the bed when you wake up. Depression. The quiet, settled conviction that you are worthless. Sexual temptation that has beaten you so many times you have stopped believing you could ever win.

I am not going to tell you the Gospel makes any of that weightless. It does not, and a counselor who says otherwise has not sat with many people. Betsie ten Boom died in Ravensbrück. The Gospel did not make the camp stop being a camp.
But here is what I do tell counselees: not one of those things reaches the bottom. The Gospel is underneath all of them.

> We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed.
— 2 Corinthians 4:8–9

Afflicted, perplexed, persecuted, struck down — Paul concedes every one. And after each one he sets a limit: not crushed, not driven to despair, not forsaken, not destroyed. The pressure is entirely real. The floor holds.
## Train your heart to remember
Here is where the work comes in, and it is work.

Nothing about your circumstances brings the Gospel to mind automatically. Grief does not do it. Exhaustion does not do it. Three o’clock in the morning certainly does not do it. Left to itself the mind runs to the trouble and stays there. Remembering has to be trained, the way any other discipline is trained.
Jeremiah shows us how. He has just spent two chapters cataloguing misery in unflinching detail — he is minimizing nothing. And then he does something deliberate:

> But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
— Lamentations 3:21–23

**This I call to mind.** That is an act of the will, performed against the current of his own feelings. He does not wait until he feels God’s mercies. He calls them to mind, and the hope follows after.

That is what I mean when I tell a counselee to **appropriate** the Gospel. Not to manufacture it — it is already true, already theirs, purchased and finished and signed. To appropriate it is to take what you already own and put it to use today.
## Fleas, soldiers, and solace

Corrie ten Boom and her sister Betsie were arrested for hiding Jews in their home in Haarlem, and were eventually sent to Ravensbrück. Their barracks was filthy and overrun with fleas. Corrie’s reaction was the human one — she wanted out. Betsie’s was to take Paul at his word and give thanks, fleas included, which struck Corrie at the time as absurd.

> Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.
— 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18

Weeks later they understood. The guards would not set foot in that barracks, because of the fleas. And because the guards stayed out, the sisters could open the Bible they had smuggled in and read it aloud to the women there, night after night, unhindered.
I do not tell that story to suggest the fleas were secretly pleasant, or that the camp was a blessing in disguise. Betsie died there. It is not a story about suffering quietly turning out to be fine.

It is a story about where a believer’s solace is located. Corrie had nothing left — no home, no freedom, no safety, and soon no sister. She had the Gospel. And the Gospel proved strong enough to hold a woman upright in Ravensbrück, surrounded by fleas and guarded by men who meant her harm.
If it will hold there, it will hold in your marriage. It will hold in your depression. It will hold at three in the morning.
## What cannot be taken from you
Paul asks the question outright, and then answers it with a list that leaves nothing out:

> Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword? … No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
— Romans 8:35, 37

> For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
— Romans 8:38–39

Notice how much Paul is willing to let into that list. Tribulation. Persecution. Famine. Sword. He never denies that these come to Christians; he assumes they do. What he denies is that any of them can reach the love of God in Christ Jesus.

That is the believer’s hope and solace, and it is why I would as gladly call this work gospel-centered counseling as Christ-centered counseling. Both names point at the same Person and the same finished work.
Nothing in your life this week is bigger than the cross, and nothing is more certain than the empty tomb. Train your heart to remember it — and then live today on what you remembered.

title: What Is Christ-Centered Biblical Counseling?
subtitle: Two convictions hold up everything else: God's Word is sufficient, and Jesus Christ is enough.
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: People often ask what makes counseling “biblical.” It is not a technique or a habit of quoting verses over problems. It rests on two convictions that are finally one conviction: God's Word is sufficient, and the Christ that Word delivers is sufficient — so you come to Him empty-handed, and He provides everything.
body: People often ask what makes counseling “biblical.” They usually expect an answer about method — that we quote verses over problems, or that we avoid certain vocabulary. But the method is downstream. Christ-centered biblical counseling rests on two convictions, and they are finally one conviction seen from two sides: God's Word is sufficient, and Jesus Christ is sufficient.
## God's Word Is Sufficient

To call Scripture sufficient is not to claim it is an encyclopedia of every subject. It is to say that on the matters it actually addresses — who you are, what has gone wrong in you, what God has done about it, and how a person is restored — it is entirely adequate. It does not need to be supplemented before it can do its work.

> All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
— 2 Timothy 3:16–17

Notice where Paul lands. Not partly equipped. Not equipped for the spiritual portion of life while something else handles the rest. **Complete, equipped for every good work.** That is a sweeping claim, and the counselor who does not believe it will always be reaching past Scripture for something with more perceived horsepower.

Job makes the same claim from the other direction — not as a theologian defending a doctrine, but as a man who had lost nearly everything and been given no explanation for any of it. In the middle of that darkness, this is what he says about the words of God:

> I have not departed from the commandment of his lips; I have treasured the words of his mouth more than my portion of food.
— Job 23:12

More than his food. Not more than his entertainment, or his opinions, or his free time — more than the thing his body could not live without. That is not a man who has been informed by Scripture. That is a man who has developed an appetite for it. Cultivating that appetite in another person is a large part of what counseling is for.
## What Happens When Someone Begins to Obey

It is an amazing thing in counseling to watch a life transform when a person begins to trust and obey God's Word. I have sat across from counselees who were cutting themselves, who were numbing their pain with substances, who came in carrying a long list of psychiatric prescriptions — and I have watched their entire lives turn around when they began to act in simple obedience and submission to what God says.

There was nothing clever about it. No technique. The change did not arrive because we finally located the right explanation for their past. It came as they trusted the God who had spoken and then did the next thing He said — and as they came to see that Jesus Christ is all they need.

That last part is not an afterthought. It is the hinge. A counselee can be taught the Bible and still be crushed by it if the Bible is handed to him as a set of demands rather than as the place where Christ is offered. Which brings us to the second conviction — which is really the first one, followed home.
## Jesus Christ Is Sufficient

Scripture is sufficient because of the One it delivers. The Word is sufficient because the Word became flesh. Take Christ out of the Bible and what remains is a standard you cannot keep and a diagnosis you cannot cure. Leave Christ in it, and every page is doing the same work: bringing an empty person to a full Savior.

> For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
— Colossians 2:9–10

**You have been filled in him.** Not you are being filled, slowly, if you apply yourself. Not you will be filled once you have made enough progress. Because of Christ, you lack nothing for your salvation and you lack nothing for your sanctification.

Put it as plainly as it can be put: **Jesus Christ is entirely enough for a person’s salvation, spiritual completeness, and daily life, requiring no human additions, good works, or alternative philosophies to reconcile someone to God.**

That last phrase is Paul’s own concern in this very chapter. Three verses before he tells us the whole fullness of deity dwells in Christ bodily, he warns the Colossians not to be taken captive “by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition … and not according to Christ” (Colossians 2:8). Sufficiency is not one doctrine sitting quietly among others. It is the first thing every rival to Christ goes after.

Most Christians will agree readily about the first half. Nothing can be added to the cross; we contributed nothing to our rescue. Then, having been saved by grace, they set about finishing the job on their own strength — as if grace got them in the door and effort has to carry them the rest of the way. Paul will not allow the split: “As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him” (Colossians 2:6). The same way in is the way on.
## Coming Empty-Handed

What a relief it is to know that we come to Christ empty-handed every day. We offer nothing — and that is precisely the good news, because it means He provides everything we need. If I had to bring something, I would have to keep bringing it, and sooner or later I would run out. An empty hand can be filled every morning.

This is what separates Christ-centered counseling from counseling that merely quotes the Bible. The goal is not a better-managed life or a person who has learned to white-knuckle his way past a besetting sin. The goal is a person who has learned to receive everything from Christ — and who therefore has somewhere to go on the day his own resources fail him again.
So what is Christ-centered biblical counseling? It is one person opening God's sufficient Word in order to bring another person to God's all-sufficient Son. Everything else is detail.

title: We Must Think With Our Own Minds
subtitle: The oldest warning about a technology of knowing is 2,400 years old, and it has never been more relevant.
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: Socrates warned that writing would give men the appearance of wisdom without the substance. We have now built the scroll that answers back. The remedy has not changed since Deuteronomy: read the primary sources, hide the Word in your own heart, and think with the mind God gave you.
body: ## A king refuses a gift

Near the end of Plato's *Phaedrus*, Socrates tells a story from Egypt. The god Theuth, inventor of number, geometry, astronomy, and letters, brings his inventions to Thamus, the king, and commends each one. When he comes to writing, he makes his boldest claim: this art, he says, will make the Egyptians wiser and improve their memories, for he has discovered a remedy for memory and wisdom.
Thamus is not impressed. The inventor of a thing, he says, is not the best judge of what it will do to the people who use it. And then he delivers a verdict that has echoed down the centuries:

> This invention will produce forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn it, because they will not practice their memory. Trusting in writing, they will recall things from external marks and not from within themselves. You have discovered a remedy not for memory but for reminding. You offer your students the appearance of wisdom, not wisdom itself; for they will read many things without instruction and will seem to know much, when for the most part they know nothing, and will be hard to get along with, having become wise in their own conceit instead of wise.
— Plato, Phaedrus 274c–275b

Socrates presses the point further. A written text, he says, is like a painting: it looks alive, but ask it a question and it "maintains a solemn silence." It cannot explain itself, cannot defend itself, cannot tell who should read it and who should not. It just rolls about, saying the same thing to everyone (275d–e). The real word, the one worth having, is the living, breathing word of the one who knows, written in the soul of the learner, of which the written word is only an image (276a).

Three charges, then. Writing weakens memory. It creates the illusion of understanding. And it cannot convey true knowledge, because true knowledge lives in a person and passes from person to person in dialogue.
## Thamus was right, and we know it because someone wrote it down

There is an irony here that Plato surely intended. We know Socrates' objection to writing only because Plato wrote it down. Socrates himself wrote nothing. Had his students shared his scruple, his name would have died with the men who heard him in the marketplace.

So Thamus was not simply right. Writing did not merely erode memory; it built libraries, preserved the law, carried the Gospel to the ends of the earth. But Thamus was not simply wrong, either. Anyone who has watched a phone number vanish from memory the moment it was saved to a contact list knows exactly what he meant. Every tool that carries a burden for us also carries away the strength we would have gained by carrying it ourselves. The question Thamus asks is not "Is this invention useful?" but "What will it do to the soul of the one who leans on it?"
That is the right question to ask about artificial intelligence.
## The text that answers back
Socrates' deepest complaint about writing was that it cannot answer questions. Ask the scroll what it means and it is silent.

We have now built the scroll that answers back. Ask it what it means and it explains. Ask it to argue the other side and it does. Ask it to summarize the *Phaedrus* and it will hand you three tidy paragraphs in under five seconds, and you will feel that you understand the *Phaedrus*.

It would be easy to conclude that AI has finally solved Socrates' problem. I think the opposite is closer to the truth. AI removes the last friction that forced us to think. The silent scroll at least made you do the work of interpretation; you had to wrestle the meaning out of it. The oracle that speaks does the wrestling for you, hands you the result, and the result feels like your own thought because it arrived in answer to your question.

This is Thamus's "remedy for reminding" at planetary scale. It is the appearance of dialogue without the labor of thought. The man who has read many things without instruction, and seems to know much, and knows nothing, and is hard to get along with, wise in his own conceit: we have all met him on the internet this week. Increasingly he is us.

I say this as someone who mines, analyzes, interprets and theologizes using human language for a living, and builds AI tools to do it. I am not against the tool. I am against what the tool will do to us if we let it think in our place.
## Words are the most powerful force in the universe
To understand why this matters so much, we have to go back further than Egypt.

"In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth." (Genesis 1:1) And how did He do it? "And God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light." (Genesis 1:3) The universe was not hammered into being. It was spoken. "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made ... For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm." (Psalm 33:6, 9) "By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God." (Hebrews 11:3)

Words are not decorations on reality. They are the instrument by which reality was made. So the question was never whether words are powerful. The question is whose words we are living on, and where those words live: on an external mark, or within.
## God told men to write
Here is where Scripture parts company with Thamus, and it is worth noticing exactly how.

God commands writing, repeatedly and explicitly. "Write this as a memorial in a book." (Exodus 17:14) The tablets of the covenant were "written with the finger of God." (Exodus 31:18) "Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you." (Jeremiah 30:2) "Write the vision; make it plain on tablets." (Habakkuk 2:2) "Write therefore the things that you have seen." (Revelation 1:19) The God who spoke the world into being wanted His words fixed on stone and parchment, so they could not be softened by memory or improved by the retelling.

But look at what He commanded alongside the writing. The king of Israel was to "write for himself in a book a copy of this law ... And it shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life." (Deuteronomy 17:18–19) Not a scribe's copy. His own hand, his own daily reading. "These words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way." (Deuteronomy 6:6–7) "This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night." (Joshua 1:8) "I have stored up your word in my heart." (Psalm 119:11)

This is God's answer to Thamus. Writing does not have to produce forgetfulness. It produces forgetfulness when it is used as a substitute for the mind. It produces wisdom when it is used to feed the mind: copied by hand, read daily, memorized, talked over at the table and on the road, written on the heart. The written Word was never meant to replace the exercised soul. It was meant to be the soul's food.
Socrates wanted the living word, written in the soul of the learner. Scripture wants that too. It simply refuses to accept that the written word and the living word are enemies.
## The Word became flesh
And then Scripture goes somewhere Socrates could not have imagined.

"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God ... All things were made through him ... And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory." (John 1:1–3, 14)

Socrates longed for a word that was alive, that could answer for itself, that could know its hearer and speak to him in particular. That Word exists. He is not a text and not a technology. He is a Person. The speech that made the universe walked into the universe and had a face.

Think of the road to Emmaus. Two disciples walking, grieving, confused. A stranger falls in beside them, and "beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself." (Luke 24:27) Afterward they say to each other, "Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?" (Luke 24:32) There is Socrates' ideal, dialogue with the one who truly knows, and there is the written Word, opened and explained. The living Word does not abolish the written word. He unlocks it.

This is why Paul can say of Christ that in Him "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." (Colossians 2:3) Not some of them. All of them. Knowledge, in its final and eternal form, is not information. It is acquaintance with a Person. The prophets "searched and inquired carefully" about the grace that was coming, and were told they were serving not themselves but us, in "things into which angels long to look." (1 Peter 1:10–12) Angels, who know more than any of us, lean forward to understand the Gospel. That is the shape of real knowledge: it is something you grow into by knowing Him, forever.
## What AI is, and what it is not
Now we can say plainly what artificial intelligence is and is not.

It is astonishingly well-informed. It has read more than any human ever will. It can retrieve, summarize, compare, and rephrase with a fluency that would have looked like sorcery to Thamus. As a remedy for reminding, it is the greatest ever built, and I use it every day.

But it is not a human being. It was not made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27). It has no soul to be regenerated, no heart on which the Word can be written, no destiny of being "conformed to the image of his Son." (Romans 8:29) It cannot behold the glory of the Lord and be "transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another." (2 Corinthians 3:18) It cannot fear the Lord, and "the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge." (Proverbs 1:7) It has read everything and understood nothing, in the only sense of understanding that lasts.

You, on the other hand, were made for exactly that. The mind you have is not a convenience to be outsourced. It is the instrument God gave you to know Him with, and the very thing He is in the process of renewing (Romans 12:2). The treasures hidden in Christ are opened to persons, not to processes. A machine can tell you what the Bible says about the resurrection. It cannot have its heart burn within it on the road.
## Read the primary sources. Think with your own mind.
So here is the practical charge, and it is not complicated.

**Read the thing itself.** Do not read a summary of the *Phaedrus*; read the *Phaedrus*. It is thirty pages. Do not let a chatbot tell you what Romans 8 means; read Romans 8, slowly, more than once, and let it argue with you. The Bereans were commended because they "examined the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so." (Acts 17:11) They checked the apostle Paul against the text. Check everything against the text, including this article.

**Do the work before you ask for help.** Form your own reading first. Then, if you like, ask the machine, and treat its answer the way you would treat a clever, well-read, spiritually dead stranger's answer: worth hearing, worth testing, never worth trusting on its own authority. "Take every thought captive to obey Christ." (2 Corinthians 10:5) That includes the thoughts that arrive fully formed from a screen.

**Write in your own hand.** Copy out a passage. Memorize it. The king was told to make his own copy for a reason. What passes through the hand and the mouth lodges in the heart in a way that what passes only through the eyes never does.

**Talk it through with a person.** Socrates was right about this much: the living word, spoken between two people who are both actually thinking, does something a text cannot. Sit at the table. Walk by the way. Teach your children. Argue with a friend.

**Know Him.** All of this is finally in service of one thing. Knowledge that does not end in Christ ends in nothing, no matter how much of it you have. "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 2:5)

Thamus was afraid that a new tool would leave men with the appearance of wisdom and none of the substance. He was speaking of marks on papyrus. We have built something far stronger, and the danger is proportionally greater. But the remedy has not changed since Deuteronomy. Write it down, yes. Then read it with your own eyes, hide it in your own heart, speak it with your own mouth, and think it through with your own mind, the mind that was made in the image of God and is being remade in the image of His Son.
No machine can do that for you. That is not a limitation of the technology. It is the glory of being made in the image of an infinitely amazing God.

title: A Covenant, Not a Contract
subtitle: What our culture's prenups reveal about marriage — and the better story Christ tells
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: A celebrity engagement put prenuptial agreements back in the headlines, and most of our culture read it as simple wisdom. But underneath the news were two completely different stories about what marriage is — and most people cannot tell you which one they are living in until a crisis forces the question.
body: A celebrity engagement made the news not long ago, and the detail that drew the most attention was not the ring or the wedding plans. It was the prenuptial agreement, and the announcement that the groom-to-be had "agreed to the terms." Much of the public read this as a kind of romantic gesture — proof of his devotion. To most of our culture, a carefully negotiated prenup is simply what wise, modern people do before they marry.

I want to be careful here, because I do not know this couple and I do not know the terms of their agreement. But the conversation around it surfaced something worth examining — not about them, but about us. Underneath the headlines were two completely different stories about what marriage is. And most people cannot tell you which story they are living in until a crisis forces the question.
## Two Stories About Marriage

The first story is that marriage is a contract. A contract is an arrangement between two parties, each protecting his or her own interests, with terms defining what each owes the other and an exit clause for when those terms are not met. A contract is, by design, a way of limiting your exposure. It assumes the relationship may end and that protecting yourself is only prudent.

The second story is that marriage is a covenant. A covenant is not a way of limiting your exposure; it is the opposite. It is the binding of two lives into one, with no exit clause, because the thing that holds it together is not performance but a promise. This is the story Scripture tells from its first pages.

> Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
— Genesis 2:24

"One flesh" is not the language of a partnership agreement. You cannot draw up terms for becoming one flesh. You cannot negotiate the fair division of one body. The image is total self-giving — two people so joined that what belongs to one belongs to the other, with nothing held back and nothing kept in reserve.

A word of honesty is needed here. There is no scriptural prohibition against a prenuptial agreement. The Bible nowhere forbids one, and we should not bind a conscience the Word leaves free. There are situations — children from a previous marriage, a family business, responsibilities a person did not choose — where godly people weigh these things and land in different places. So the question Scripture presses is not really about the document. It is about the story underneath it. A signed agreement can sit on top of a covenant heart, and a beautiful ceremony can hide a contract heart. What God searches is which of the two stories you are actually living in.
## Where the Covenant Comes From

Why would anyone live that way? Why surrender every protection, hold nothing back, and bind yourself to another person for life with no way out? The answer is that the covenant of marriage was never meant to stand on its own. It was always pointing to something beyond itself.

> "Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh." This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.
— Ephesians 5:31–32

Paul takes the oldest description of marriage and tells us what it was always about. Marriage is a living picture of the way Christ loves His church. And that love is the furthest thing from a contract. Christ did not enter a carefully negotiated arrangement with His people, hedged against the risk of our failure. He bound Himself to a people who brought nothing to the table, who could not perform, who had no assets worth protecting, and who betrayed Him again and again — and He held to the covenant anyway, at infinite cost to Himself.

Richard Sibbes put it simply: "Christ betroths the church to himself in mercy." Not in exchange for performance. In mercy. That is the model marriage was made to reflect: a faithfulness that does not depend on the other person earning it. It is no accident that God so often describes His own relationship to His people as a marriage, or that their wandering grieves Him the way betrayal grieves a faithful spouse. The whole Bible is, in one sense, the story of a God who refuses to protect Himself from the cost of loving us.
## The Story Your Counselee Is Already Living

Many counselees have absorbed the contract story without ever choosing it. They learned it from a parent's divorce, from a betrayal they never recovered from, from a culture that calls self-protection wisdom. They are not cynics. They are afraid. And the prenup, whether it is written on paper or only carried in the heart, is fear wearing the costume of prudence.

You do not help such a person by scolding them for their fear or arguing with them about celebrities. You help them by surfacing the fear gently, and then telling them a better story — the only story strong enough to make covenant love possible. A person will risk being fully known, with no exit plan, only after they have first been loved that way. And that love has a name.
## Questions Worth Considering

Whether you are a counselor sitting with someone who is wrestling with marriage, or simply willing to examine your own heart, these are the kinds of questions that bring the real story to the surface. They are not meant to be fired off in sequence like an interrogation. They are questions to hold in your mind and ask gently, as doors open.

*When you imagine a healthy marriage, what does it look like? What would have to happen for you to feel you needed to leave?* Questions like these surface what a person actually believes marriage is, long before a single verse is opened.

*What are you most afraid would happen if you held nothing back — no exit plan, no safety net? Where does that fear come from?* Get underneath the logic of self-protection and you will usually find an old wound: a trust that was broken, a marriage that failed, a quiet conviction that no one is finally safe to be fully known by.

*If marriage cost you everything and gave you nothing back, would it still be worth it?* The answer tells you what a person is really trusting in — financial security, independence, control, reputation. The idol will name itself if you ask the right question.

*Have you ever felt that God was holding something back from you, protecting Himself from the cost of loving you?* How a person experiences God's faithfulness and how they approach human intimacy are almost never unrelated. Someone who does not trust God's covenant love will struggle to live it out toward a spouse.

*If God had entered a prenup with us — protecting Himself against the risk of our failure — where would that leave you and me?* This is the question that turns the whole conversation toward the gospel.
## The Love That Makes Self-Protection Unnecessary

In the end, no one is argued into covenant marriage. People are not persuaded to stop protecting themselves; they are freed from the need to. And that freedom comes from one place only: an encounter with the love of a God who entered covenant with us at infinite personal cost and has never once moved to protect Himself from us.

He knew exactly what loving us would cost. He saw the betrayal coming. And He held fast anyway. That is the marriage every human marriage was made to picture, and it is the only love strong enough to make us willing to hold nothing back.
"Christ betroths the church to himself in mercy." Help a person feel the weight of that love, and the exit clauses quietly lose their appeal.

title: Jesus, Breaker of Boundaries
subtitle: Better than boundaries — limitations, love, and wisdom
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: Counselees often ask for help “setting healthy boundaries.” But Scripture offers something deeper and more demanding than a self-drawn circle — limitations, love, and wisdom, and a Lord who broke down every dividing wall.
body: A frequent request from counselees struggling with difficult relationships or the strain of managing life is for help "setting healthy boundaries." The language of "boundaries" has become a fixture of the Christian vocabulary, and drawing them is widely regarded as a mark of wisdom and maturity. Boundaries are often described as defining what is yours and what is not, so that you can "own your life and choices"—a self-drawn circle enclosing you and whatever you value, with others invited to draw their own. It is an appealing and remarkably flexible idea.

Consider the situations in which people reach for boundaries: physical exhaustion or emotional overwhelm; chronic anger or resentment; an inability to say "no"; poor habits of body and soul; an inability to speak the truth in love; relationships without mutual care and service; feeling controlled by the opinions and desires of others; being driven mainly by guilt or fear. These are real burdens, and the people who carry them are not wrong to long for relief. The question is whether "boundaries" is the answer Scripture actually gives.
## Is "Boundaries" a Biblical Idea?

Some episodes in our Lord's life seem to commend the wisdom of limits. He tended His body's needs, sleeping peacefully through a storm (Mark 4:37–39). He guarded His communion with the Father, withdrawing to pray though the crowds pressed in (Luke 5:15–16). He refused the agenda others pressed on Him, declining to be made an earthly king (John 6:15). And though He came to lay down His life, He did so according to the Father's appointed plan, not the will of men, at times withdrawing from those who sought His harm (Luke 9:10).

And yet the deeper truth is that Jesus, from first to last, broke down every dividing wall (Eph. 2:14). He crossed the boundary of heaven itself to become man and dwell among us. The only person who ever had the right to wall Himself off from sinners instead ate with them, touched and was touched by lepers and prostitutes and the unclean, spoke with a Samaritan woman of loose reputation, overturned the temple tables, forgave sins, healed on the Sabbath, and declared that He and the Father are one. He commended a Samaritan who entangled himself in a stranger's trouble rather than minding his own affairs, and He charged His followers to love their enemies rather than fortify themselves against them. This is not the portrait of a man managing a tidy, self-protective circle.

So we should be cautious about baptizing "boundaries" as a biblical command. It is, at best, a modern category we must hold up to the light of God's Word—and at worst, a Christianized version of the autonomous self.
## You Are Not Your Own

Here is where the boundaries model most needs examining. Its foundational instinct is ownership: define what is yours, take back control, "own your life." But Scripture confronts the believer with a different and better word: "You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body" (1 Cor. 6:19–20). "None of us lives to himself… we are the Lord's" (Rom. 14:7–8). As the old catechism confesses, our only comfort in life and in death is that "I am not my own, but belong—body and soul, in life and in death—to my faithful Savior, Jesus Christ."

This changes everything. The Christian's life is not a circle to be defended but a life that has been purchased, claimed, and now belongs to Another. Our chief end is not to secure and curate what is ours, but to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever. A counselee who learns only to draw firmer lines around the self may simply trade one bondage for another—exchanging the tyranny of others' demands for the tyranny of self-rule.

There is a better way, and it is more demanding, more nuanced, and more faithful than a single word can hold. Scripture braids together three strands—**limitations, love, and wisdom**—and it is in their interplay that holiness and health grow. (This three-fold framework follows Brenda Pauken, ["Better Than Boundaries"](https://www.biblicalcounselingcoalition.org/2021/02/05/better-than-boundaries/), Biblical Counseling Coalition, 2021).
## Limitations

We are creatures, not the Creator. God has appointed limits to our time, strength, knowledge, and ability; our bodies are subject to weakness, decay, and death. To rage against the realities of our finitude—to refuse sleep, rest, nourishment, and ordinary care—is not devotion but a quiet contempt for the way God made us. Stewarding the gift of life means honoring the limits the Lord has built into it.

To honor our limits is also to confess that we are not sovereign—God is. There are no outcomes we can guarantee. When a hard relationship does not change, it is easy to conclude we must have failed; but we are not called to produce the change, only to labor faithfully and leave the increase to God (1 Cor. 3:6–7). His sovereignty frees us from the crushing weight of results that were never ours to carry.

Honoring limits will also require saying "no" to some genuinely good things that are simply not ours to do in this season. If that proves nearly impossible, the cause may not be love at all but people-pleasing, a savior complex, an identity built on usefulness, or a quiet failure to trust the God who actually governs the world. Our motives need rigorous, prayerful examination, for the heart is deceitful above all things (Jer. 17:9).
## Love

A focus on limits, left to itself, can curdle into the very self-love, self-focus, and self-protection that our sin already inclines us toward. So limitation must be governed by love—love that is the opposite of a defended boundary, a giving of oneself, by grace, beyond what we thought we could bear. Such love does not originate in us; it flows from the wildly unbalanced love we have received from God in Christ: "We love because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19).

But we must let Scripture, not the therapeutic culture, define love—because it is easy to baptize sentiment or self-interest with that holy word. And here our Lord is startlingly concrete: **"If you love me, you will keep my commandments"** (John 14:15; cf. 14:21; 15:10; 1 John 5:3). Jesus does not leave love to be defined by feeling, by self-expression, or by what protects us. He weds love to obedience—to the commandments of God. And the whole law, in turn, is summed up in love to God and love to neighbor (Matt. 22:37–40), so that the commandments are not the enemy of love but its very shape and content. To ask "How do I love this difficult person?" is therefore to ask "What does God's revealed will require of me toward them?"—not "Where do I draw the line?"

This reframes everything the boundaries model tries to address. Scripture never moves from the command to love to a psychological category like "boundaries"; it presses us instead to ask what it looks like to love a hard person according to God's commandments.

And godly love, defined by the law, is robust. It confronts evil rather than ignoring it (Lev. 19:17; Matt. 18:15). It perseveres and forgives (1 Cor. 13:7; Col. 3:13). It refuses to repay evil for evil, blessing even those who persecute (1 Pet. 3:9; Rom. 12:17–21). It does not interfere with God's just pattern of sowing and reaping (Gal. 6:7). It is willing to risk another's displeasure rather than please, placate, and pretend. It will not do for others what they can and should do for themselves, when "helping" only feeds laziness, entitlement, and self-absorption (2 Thess. 3:10). And it rescues people from their folly, as Abigail's intervention rescued both David and Nabal (1 Sam. 25:3–35).

Because we are secure in God's love for us in Christ, we are freed to seek another's true good ahead of our own comfort—just as Christ "made himself nothing," took the limits of a servant, and laid down His rights to save us (Phil. 2:5–8). And precisely because love is defined by God's commandments and aims at another's good, the most loving act toward an unrepentant or abusive person may be to deny him the opportunity to go on sinning against us. Limiting contact, in such cases, is not the self-protective circle of the boundaries model; it is obedience—a refusal to enable sin, a guarding against further harm, and an act of hope for the relationship's eventual restoration through repentance.
## Wisdom

Honoring our limits and loving as the law commands is never formulaic; it is the work of wisdom, which holds the two together under the fear of the Lord. Wisdom weighs our call to love as God loves, our creaturely limits in this season, the particular temptations to sin and self that each of us carries, and the actual person and need set before us.

Wisdom is the labor of a lifetime, but the means of grace are appointed for it. First, sit under the whole counsel of God's Word, not a favored slice of it, so that you are not left with lopsided answers. Look for the tensions Scripture holds together—justice and mercy, God's sovereignty and our responsibility, our limits and our calling to love—and let them keep you from simplistic solutions that flatter the self.

Second, do not go it alone. God has given the church. Mature brothers and sisters can expose our blind spots, lend perspective our own hearts are too biased to see, and bear our burdens with us (Gal. 6:2).

Finally, commune with God Himself. Wisdom is not finally a set of propositions but a knowing of the Lord (Prov. 9:10). What the struggling counselee most needs is not a static formula extracted from God but a living walk with Him. Our relationships are not problems to be solved and sealed off behind well-drawn lines; they are the very ground on which, by the Spirit, we are conformed to Christ—reflecting His patience, His long-suffering, and His relentless, pursuing love for sinners like us.

title: Grace in the Furnace
subtitle: How suffering shapes us into vessels of Christ
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: The potter does not despise the cracked clay. He sees in every fracture an opportunity — a place where his hands can press deeper, where the fire can do its refining work.
body: The potter does not despise the cracked clay. He sees in every fracture an opportunity — a place where his hands can press deeper, where the fire can do its refining work. Biblical counseling begins here: not with solutions, but with a theology of the kiln.

Romans 8:28 is often quoted as a comfort verse, deployed quickly in the presence of grief as though the pain were an embarrassment to be expedited. But Paul's argument is richer and more demanding. He does not promise that all things are good; he promises that God works all things together for good to those who are called according to his purpose.

That purpose (prothesis) is not vague. Paul defines it immediately: to be conformed to the image of his Son. Conformity to Christ is the furnace's aim. The counselor's task, then, is not to remove the heat but to help the sufferer understand what the heat is for.

This does not minimize pain. It dignifies it. When we tell a grieving mother that her loss is purposeless randomness, we offer her nothing but a cold universe. When we tell her it is being shaped by a Father who gave his own Son, we give her something to stand on even in the ash.

title: Social Media and the Distracted Soul
subtitle: Reclaiming attention as an act of worship
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: Attention is not a neutral faculty. Scripture treats it as a worshipful act. What we behold, we become — and the architecture of social media is designed to fragment beholding into an infinite scroll of competing claimants for the soul.
body: Attention is not a neutral faculty. Scripture treats it as a worshipful act. What we behold, we become — and the architecture of social media is designed to fragment beholding into an infinite scroll of competing claimants for the soul.

Psalm 115 draws the oldest connection between idolatry and transformation: those who make idols become like them. The idol of the social feed is not stone but pixel — yet the dynamic is identical. It promises significance (likes), belonging (followers), and identity (personal brand). These are not trivial desires. They are the desires that only Christ can fill.

Biblical counseling in this space must resist two failures: the moralistic (just stop using it) and the therapeutic (set healthy screen limits). Both treat the behavior without the heart. The deeper question is always: what does this person believe social media can give them that they cannot find in Christ?

The goal is not Luddism. It is liturgical reordering — helping the counselee rebuild a life of attention whose center of gravity is Word, prayer, and embodied community, rather than the dopamine pulse of notification.

title: Come to Me, All Who Labor
subtitle: The yoke of Christ as rest, not burden
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: The invitation of Matthew 11:28 is the strangest paradox in the Gospels. Jesus calls the weary to take on a yoke. Rest is found not in the removal of burden but in the exchange of burdens.
body: The invitation of Matthew 11:28 is the strangest paradox in the Gospels. Jesus calls the weary to take on a yoke. Rest is found not in the removal of burden but in the exchange of burdens — from the crushing weight of self-justification to the gentle load of grace.

First-century listeners heard yoke as a rabbinic metaphor for Torah observance and discipleship. Every teacher had a yoke — his interpretive school, his demands, his system. Jesus is not abolishing yokes; he is contrasting his yoke with every other. I am gentle and lowly in heart, he says. No rabbi before him ever described himself that way.

The weariness Jesus addresses is not primarily physical. It is the exhaustion of performing for an audience that is never satisfied. The yoke of Christ is a transfer of jurisdiction: from the court of human opinion to the verdict already spoken at the cross.

In counseling, we meet this weariness constantly. The anxious man who cannot rest because he cannot prove his worth. The perfectionistic woman who serves God as though grace had a co-pay. The gospel addresses not their behavior but their court. Christ has already spoken the verdict: Beloved.

title: The Counselor as Barnabas
subtitle: Encouragement as a theological act
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: Barnabas means son of encouragement — yet that title was given, not born. His name was Joseph. The church renamed him for what he did, and what he did was see potential in people others had written off. This is the counselor's vocation.
body: Barnabas means son of encouragement — yet that title was given, not born. His name was Joseph. The church renamed him for what he did, and what he did was see potential in people others had written off. This is the counselor's vocation.

The Greek word paraklesis — encouragement, exhortation, comfort — shares its root with parakletos, the word Jesus uses for the Holy Spirit. This is not accidental. Encouragement, at its depth, is the Spirit's work expressed through human presence. The counselor does not manufacture hope; he mediates it.

Barnabas appears at two critical junctures: he vouches for the feared Saul to a suspicious Jerusalem church, and he later refuses to abandon John Mark when Paul would. In both cases, he extends trust to the person others found disqualifying. This is not naivety. It is a theology of second chances rooted in the God who restored Peter.

Good biblical counseling looks for what God is still doing in a person, not merely cataloging what has broken. It asks: what does redemption look like here? What does resurrection look like, in this particular life, at this particular moment?

title: Anxiety and the Sovereignty of God
subtitle: Why Philippians 4:6 is not a command to simply calm down
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: Philippians 4:6 is one of the most quoted and most misapplied verses in pastoral ministry. Do not be anxious about anything is read as a command to stop feeling anxious — as though anxiety were simply a moral failure correctable by willpower.
body: Philippians 4:6 is one of the most quoted and most misapplied verses in pastoral ministry. Do not be anxious about anything is read as a command to stop feeling anxious — as though anxiety were simply a moral failure correctable by willpower. Paul's meaning is richer and more merciful than that.

The word translated be anxious (merimnao) carries the sense of a divided mind — a heart pulled in multiple directions by competing concerns. Paul is not condemning the anxious person; he is diagnosing a condition and prescribing a reorientation: In everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.

Notice the structure: the antidote to divided attention is not focused attention on one's own feelings but directed speech toward God. The anxious person is not told to think less about their problem; they are told to bring the problem to the One who holds all things. Prayer is the transfer of burden.

This is why the passage ends not with your anxiety will disappear but with the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds. The peace comes after the prayer — and it is a peace that outpaces comprehension, meaning the circumstances may not change, but the orientation of the heart does.

title: Help! I'm Spending Too Much Time on Social Media!
subtitle: Walking wisely in a culture engineered for distraction
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: You didn't plan to spend an hour on TikTok. You never do. But the algorithm is patient. Few passages speak more directly to this than Ephesians 5:8–17.
body: You did not plan to spend an hour on TikTok. You never do. But the algorithm is patient, and it seems that it knows you better than you know yourself. If you are a Christian with a smartphone, this article is for you.

Few passages speak more directly to it than Ephesians 5:8–17. Written to believers living in the spiritually dark and sexually permissive city of Ephesus, Paul's words cut to the heart of what it means to walk faithfully in a culture bent on distraction and indulgence.
## Three Key Exhortations
Three exhortations emerge from this passage that speak directly to the challenge of social media:
Do not partner with sin (vv. 7–8) — instead, walk in the light (v. 9). Discern what is pleasing to the Lord (v. 10). Walk wisely, redeeming your time, "because the days are evil" (v. 16).
## Do Not Partner with Sin

Algorithms are engineered to entice — to surface content that is sexually charged, that stokes envy, or that keeps you scrolling for one more hit of outrage or entertainment. When you indulge a creator's sinful content, you are not a passive observer. You are contributing to their platform and livelihood. In a very real sense, you are partnering with them in their sin.

> "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?"
— Jeremiah 17:9
## Be Discerning

Social media has a remarkable ability to dull our spiritual senses over time. Even seemingly harmless content can quietly crowd out the things of God when consumed without discretion. An unchecked diet of partisan news can shift our gaze from the eternal to the anxious, training us to think of ourselves as citizens of a political tribe rather than citizens of the Kingdom.
## Redeem the Time
Before you open an app, ask yourself honestly: How will this end? An hour from now, will I be more joyful? More prayerful? More ready to serve my neighbor and love my Savior?

> "Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil."
— Ephesians 5:15–16

God has purposes for your one life. You are called to carry the good news of the gospel to the people around you, to love your family, to build up the church. Every hour surrendered to an algorithm is an hour not given to those things. The days are indeed evil — but they are also short. Use them well.

title: Conquering Anger by GRACE
subtitle: Remembering what God has already done in Christ
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: Sinful anger is an emotion rooted in pride, selfishness, or a desire for revenge. It manifests as outbursts, bitterness, and malice — what Scripture calls "wrath" or "rage."
body: ## What Is Sinful Anger?
Sinful anger is an emotion rooted in pride, selfishness, or a desire for revenge. It manifests as outbursts, bitterness, and malice — what Scripture often calls "wrath" or "rage."

> "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel."
— James 4:1–2
## How Is This Different from God's Anger?
God's anger is perfectly justified and perfectly controlled. Human anger is frequently sinful, prone to foolishness, and often leads to evil action.
## Guidelines for Overcoming Sinful Anger
### 1. Remember That God Is in Control

> "Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases."
— Psalm 115:3

> "No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape."
— 1 Corinthians 10:13
### 2. Remember That You Are Not God

> "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord."
— Romans 12:19
### 3. Remember Who You Are in Christ

> "Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come."
— 2 Corinthians 5:17
### 4. Remember God's Graciousness to You — and Pass It On

> "Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you."
— Ephesians 4:31–32

The Parable of the Unforgiving Servant powerfully illustrates this point. A servant forgiven an incalculable debt turns and refuses to forgive a fellow servant a trivial one. The grace we have received is the measure by which we are called to extend grace to others.

title: Emotions in Biblical Counseling
subtitle: Letting Scripture inform our feelings, not the other way around
author: Jeff Johnson
excerpt: Emotions are a window into a person's heart, enabling a counselor to gauge spiritual maturity, integrity, and the fruit of the Spirit.
body: Emotions are a window into a person's heart, enabling a counselor to gauge spiritual maturity, integrity, and the fruit of the Spirit. Counselors should allow emotions to surface freely, while taking care not to encourage or validate those that are sinful. The fruits of the Spirit listed in Galatians 5:22–23 serve as the primary gauge of righteous emotion.

> "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?"
— Jeremiah 17:9

Robert Robinson recognized this same reality when he wrote in 1758, "Prone to wander, Lord, I feel it, prone to leave the God I love." What Robinson confessed, genuine believers across the centuries have echoed — our hearts, as the seat of our emotions, require constant renewal from the Lord.
## The Spirit's Work in the Heart

Counselees are ultimately helpless apart from the Spirit's work in their lives. When a counselee cannot seem to gain control over lust, anger, or similar besetting emotions, this may indicate they are not yet united to Christ.
